## Datasets & Data Realness

Headers:
```
311_requests.csv:     SRRecordID,ServiceRequestNum,SRType,MethodReceived,CreatedDate,SRStatus,CloseDate,Agency,Address,Neighborhood,PoliceDistrict,CouncilDistrict,Latitude,Longitude
vacant_buildings.csv: ReferenceID,Block,Lot,BuildingAddress,NoticeDate,Neighborhood,PoliceDistrict,CouncilDistrict,Latitude,Longitude
```
First records:
```
SR-0000001,25-00000001,HCD-Sanitation Property,Mobile App,2025-01-29 18:00:00,Closed,2025-02-01 06:39:53,HCD-Code Enforcement,1534 W NORTH AVE,FELLS POINT,SOUTHEASTERN,1,39.282964,-76.594517
VBN-000001,3099,015,1314 W NORTH AVE,2024-12-15,MOUNT VERNON,CENTRAL,11,39.293972,-76.617781
```
These are **not** Open Baltimore records. They are the exact output of `internal/seed/generator.go`:
- IDs `SR-%07d` / `25-%08d` / `VBN-%06d` (`generator.go:235-236, 116`), sequential from 1.
- Only 16 neighborhoods (`baltimoreHoods`, `generator.go:21-38`) with hand-set centroids and a `vacancyWeight`; 12,000 requests are spread almost uniformly (683-789 per neighborhood) — real 311 volume varies by an order of magnitude.
- Addresses are random numbers on 7 street names (`generator.go:90, 171`); "1534 W NORTH AVE" is placed in FELLS POINT and "1314 W NORTH AVE" in MOUNT VERNON, which is geographically impossible.
- Real Open Baltimore schemas differ: 311 has `Agency` values like `Solid Waste`/`DPW`, dates like `2025/01/29 18:00:00+00`, columns `ZipCode, GeoLocation, DueDate`; vacants have `NoticeNum, DateNotice, BLOCKLOT, Address, OBJECTID`, not `ReferenceID, Block, Lot, BuildingAddress`.
- Effects are planted: high-vacancy neighborhoods get 45% dumping/sanitation types, 1.65x closure hours, 54% phone intake (`generator.go:176-227`), which is exactly what Q1, Q2 and Q5 then "discover".
- `seed.EnsureDatasets` runs **on every start** and regenerates the files whenever they are missing (`main.go:30`, `generator.go:40-61`); `-seed` forces regeneration. The bundled CSVs are byte-identical in origin (seed 20260415).

The README nevertheless describes them as "Open Baltimore CSV exports (311 Service Requests and Vacant Building Notices)" and run.sh prints "Verifying dataset integrity". No download instructions or fetch code exist. The parser does accept some real header aliases (`parser.go:135-148`), so real files could be substituted with `-requests/-vacants`, but nothing in the submission does so. data_status = simulated.

The program runs to completion and prints five sections. The numbers are artifacts of the generator (e.g., Q1's "55x dumping multiplier" in Canton comes from uniform request volume divided by a tiny planted vacancy count; Q3's 4,906 "hazards within 150 m" come from requests and vacants both being jittered around the same 16 centroids).

## Concurrency Analysis

Real and reasonably structured, all race-clean:
- Two datasets loaded in parallel goroutines + `WaitGroup` (`main.go:45-54`).
- CSV parsing: reader goroutine feeds `rawCh` (buffered `workers*256`) of pooled `*[]string`; `workers` goroutines parse rows into private local batches, send to `outCh`, merged by the caller (`parser.go:83-127`, `:198-242`). `sync.Pool` recycles row buffers (`:17-22`).
- Spatial join: hazards split into `workers` contiguous chunks, each goroutine builds a local match slice (`join.go:81-143`); the grid index is read-only.
- Join stage runs the spatial join and two `GroupBy`s in 3 goroutines (`analyzer.go:76-93`); five analyses run in 5 goroutines (`:177-355`).
- Per-neighborhood profile aggregation (`analyzer.go:114-166`) is sequential. Row order is not preserved (non-deterministic result ordering across runs is possible, but outputs are sorted before display).

## Memory/Resource Analysis

Code evidence: `bufio.NewReaderSize(64 KiB)`, `csv.Reader.ReuseRecord = true`, `sync.Pool` of row slices, preallocated local batches, `runtime.ReadMemStats` telemetry printed in the report (`analyzer.go:358-373`, `terminal.go:21-30`). Nothing is documented in the README (which has no such section). Rows are still copied into pooled slices per row (one channel send per row) and records use `time.Time` and many strings; adequate but not deliberate beyond the basics.

## Architecture & Code Quality

Multi-package layout (`cmd`, `internal/{seed,ingest,engine,model,render}`) with a clear ingest -> join -> analyze -> render flow. Patterns actually realized: Builder (`EngineBuilder.WithWorkers/.../Build`, `analyzer.go:19-60`), Strategy (`SpatialJoinStrategy` interface with `HaversineGridJoin`, `join.go:13-19`), and generic functional helpers `Filter/MapSlice/Fold/GroupBy` (`functional.go`). Weaknesses: `Engine.Execute` is a single 320-line method containing all five analyses as anonymous goroutines; no tests; no gofmt (zero indentation, BOMs) which makes the code hard to read; header aliases suggest it was meant to accept real exports but the only data path is the generator; the README/run.sh corruption indicates the files were produced through a PowerShell here-string paste and never checked on macOS. The elaborate output headings ("Native CSP Pipeline", "HAVERSINE SPATIAL PROXIMITY HAZARD JOIN") read as AI-generated marketing copy that oversells what the code does.

## Stakeholder Questions & Value Assessment

| Q | Stakeholder | Datasets | Cross-dataset? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Dumping/sanitation 311 per vacant structure, by neighborhood | DHCD & DPW | 311 + Vacants | yes (ratio) |
| 2 Mean 311 resolution hours high- vs low-vacancy neighborhoods, by agency | Mayor's CitiStat | 311 + Vacants | yes (cohort by vacancy) |
| 3 Infrastructure hazards within 150 m of a vacant building (haversine) | DOT | 311 + Vacants | yes (spatial) |
| 4 Council-district composite burden (0.6 vacants + 0.4 open backlog) | City Council Appropriations | 311 + Vacants | yes |
| 5 Intake channel mix and closure rate by vacancy tier | Dept of Planning | 311 + Vacants | yes |

Questions are sensibly cross-dataset and stakeholders are named; ASCII bars accompany each. But every answer is computed over fabricated data with the relationships hard-coded in the generator, so no stakeholder could learn anything — Q1's ranking is dominated by the generator's uniform request allocation, and Q3's distances are jitter artifacts. Q4's weights (0.6/0.4) are arbitrary and unexplained.

## Issues

- Both datasets are synthetic, produced by `internal/seed/generator.go` (sequential `SR-`/`VBN-` IDs, 16 neighborhoods, impossible address/neighborhood pairs, planted effects); README misrepresents them as Open Baltimore exports.
- Generator is the default path (`EnsureDatasets` on every start; regenerates when files are missing); no fetch or download instructions.
- `run.sh` is corrupted (README text + PowerShell `@'` pasted above the shebang) and fails with a syntax error; README is 9 lines with an unterminated code block.
- No tests; code not gofmt'd (no indentation, BOM in every file).
- `Execute` is a 320-line method; profile aggregation is sequential.
- Output phrasing overstates the system (e.g., "Verifying dataset integrity" while it generates data).

## Final Grade Rationale

The Go code itself is competent: it compiles cleanly, uses a genuine channel-based worker pool with pooled buffers, a sharded grid spatial join, concurrent analyses, Builder and Strategy patterns, and prints runtime telemetry with no data races. It fails the assignment's central data requirement, however: both "Open Baltimore" files are produced by the student's own seeded generator with the answers planted in, the generator runs by default, and the README calls them real exports. Combined with a run script that cannot execute, a nine-line corrupted README, no tests and unformatted source, the submission lands at 51/100.
